Mr. Chairman, I have a few observations to make on this item. The other day when I spoke on item No. 1 of the minister's estimates I had just started to say something about the great value of small public works that require very little planning and very little advance organization. It so happens that all around the coast of Newfoundland and particularly in my riding there are many such works that are still very badly needed.
It is true that in the nine years since confederation the most urgent works have been done. But there was, as the minister knows, a long period before that when, first because of economic difficulties and then because of the war, marine works such as wharves, break-waters, slipways and other services, which under confederation the federal government has the responsibility for supplying, were seriously neglected, and I think I will offend nobody by saying that. The result is that, despite the magnificent and untiring efforts of the minister's department over the last nine years, there is still a great deal of this work to be done, as the minister is well aware. As I said the other day, part of the reason that more has not been done in the last few years is that the availability of supervisory personnel, engineers and engineers' assistants, was so limited that the department simply could not redouble its efforts.
But, at a time like this when, according to the latest figures we have been given, 24 per cent of the working force of Newfoundland is unemployed, surely something extra could be done. Those are figures which the bureau of statistics gives us, so no hon. members should suggest I am exaggerating. We are hoping that when the figures come out for May they will not be quite so bad. The improvement, as I know from having been there only last week, is not anything like as encouraging as we would like it to be. Anything the minister can do to speed things up this year, or toward planning for next year, would be very welcome indeed.
I have told the minister twice, and I do not think it will do me any harm to say a third time, that I welcome his suggestion he is going to build a real shelf. I have a few items that I should like him to put on the shelf. I believe the simplest way would be to start systematically at one end of my

riding and go through it very quickly. It will be an interesting tour, and it would make me happy if the minister would come along and make the tour with me.
On your boat?
I do not know whether or not that would be the minister's idea of a holiday, but I am quite sure if he did it he would be completely convinced.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would there be a real sailor on board to look after the ship?
Yes, and I can assure the minister there would not only be a good sailor on board but a good cook as well. The minister looks as though the ministrations of a good cook would not do him any harm.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I have gained 20 pounds since I got over here.
I can assure the minister that his experience is not the experience we had when we were over there. We worked so hard we lost weight.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You lost more than weight.

Happily at any rate, in my case I did not lose a very important part of my anatomy, my seat.
Being here as a representative of the constituency of Bonavista-Twillingate I feel that my constituents would expect me to indicate some of the more urgent of these marine works that the minister could undertake. We would all be grateful if he were able to undertake them, if not this year, then next year, and in some cases it might take a little longer than that.
I am going to start at Twillingate, which is one of the largest and also one of the most historic fishing settlements in Canada, there are 35 families. At Bluff Head cove, Twillingate in addition to the main harbour. As the minister is undoubtedly aware, a considerable dredging operation has been under way, perhaps I should say was under way for a while but was suspended because of what was felt to be a more urgent need at Port-aux-Basques. I have no complaint about that. However, I do hope, at the earliest possible date, the minister will find it possible to have the main dredging operation at Twillingate resumed.
In addition to that there is the need for a breakwater at Jenkins' cove to protect the fishermen's boats. I may say there are about 75 fishing families involved there. A similar breakwater is needed at Ragged point, where there are 35 families. At Bluff Head cove, there are about 35 fishermen, most of them heads of families. In addition to that, the
Supply-Public Works minister's department did an excellent job last year with a bulldozer dredging one of the coves in Twillingate. This was a relatively small job, but the appreciation of those fishermen would touch the minister's heart deeply if he had a chance of meeting them.
There are several other coves, Jenkins' cove, Durrell Bottom Maidment and Hillier's Bottom, and Shoal Tickle, where only a little dredging with a bulldozer would improve the situation immensely. Then, moving from Twillingate island to New World island, it is true that the main settlements at New World island have excellent wharves, but there are a number of smaller places where wharves are needed. Bridgeport, Tizzard's Harbour, Hillgrade and Carter's Cove, are places that just come to my mind quickly on thinking it over.
In addition to that, there is a small dredging operation which I would hope the minister might find it possible to get done at Whales Gulch. I am very glad to see that it is proposed to go on this year and finish the Pikes Arm canal, because it is going to be of immense advantage to the fishermen in that area. I may say that, when I was there on other business in March, I saw the new wharf at Birchy bay, and the lobster fishermen especially are tremendously pleased with that wharf. However, like Oliver Twist, they would like a little more. They would like another block on the wharf so that they would be able to reach deeper water. Then, Boyd's cove is an important place. It is a jumping-off place for the islands and it very badly needs a wharf. If this would touch the minister's heart any more, I would say that Boyd's cove was one of the few places where I did not get a majority, so perhaps the minister would undertake to build a wharf there right away.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What did the hon. member say they needed there?

A wharf; this would be a relatively expensive wharf, but it is very badly needed. Then, a smaller wharf is needed at Port Albert. Port Albert is at the end of the line of the road being built, and when the road is built a good part of the traffic to Change islands and to Fogo island will come up the road from Lewisporte to Port Albert and by boat across to these islands. In addition to providing for the needs of the fishermen, such a wharf would provide for the needs of the traffic both of persons and of freight.
Then, going into Gander bay, there is a perennial problem of getting a coastal wharf at Gander Bay. The minister's officials will tell him what a vexing problem this is, and

Supply-Public Works if the minister can solve it we will all be very grateful. There are, in addition, two or three places in Gander bay, the Gander Bay settlement itself, Main Point and Davidsville, where landing wharves would be of immense help to the people. Then, there is a wharf at Frederickton, which is well known to the minister's officials. This is the Frederickton in Newfoundland, of course. At Frederickton, the view in the community is that a small block at the end of the wharf is what is needed. I do not presume to offer a professional opinion on that, but there is an improvement needed at Frederickton. Then, at Carmanville there is one of the greatest antiquities in Newfoundland and one of the longest wharves. I do hope the minister's department will get around to replacing it before it collapses entirely. Carmanville is a big and growing settlement and this is a great need of the people.
Then, going back to Change islands, there is a long standing need for a wharf. This is an important fishing settlement as well as an important place of transit. In the greater part of Fogo island wharves have been built recently. At Seldom Come By, the minister's department has done a wonderful job, and at Fogo itself there is a relatively new wharf. At Joe Batt's Arm there is a new wharf, but they would like an improvement to the wharf.
At Tilting a small wharf would be very helpful. But the place I should like to appeal for most of all is a place sometimes called Deep Bay and sometimes called Hare Bay- that is near Fogo-where the people have no place to land at all. It is a very hard place. It is a place where one could not build a very large structure. But there are a good many fishermen there and they encounter great difficulty. At times it is impossible for them to launch their boats and get them into the water.
Then going back to the straight shore, I understand the minister is planning to go ahead this year with the breakwater at Aspen Cove and I hope with some dredging as well at Ladle Cove. There is a need for a slipway for the fishermen at Ragged harbour. There is a petition that I believe the minister received-I know the Minister of Fisheries did -for a breakwater at Flin Point at Musgrave harbour. One of the leading merchants of Musgrave harbour is a very well known and celebrated person in Newfoundland named Mr. James Way who on one occasion contested an election in Newfoundland for the minister's party against the premier of Newfoundland. Mr. Way has said he would build a fish plant if the minister would build this breakwater. I commend this project to the minister's sympathetic consideration.
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

Then there is a certain amount of dredging needed at Deadman's Bay. I am pleased to say that the minister is going to build a wharf this year at Lumsden North. At Lums-den South what is needed is a breakwater. Lumsden is one of the greatest fishing settlements in the world and it has some of the finest fishermen in the world but it is a terribly open place. If this breakwater could be constructed, it would be a tremendous boom to these fine God-fearing people. Then we come to Cape Freels.

May I ask
the hon. member a question?
Certainly.
What did the Liberal party do when they were in power?

If the hon. member for Hamilton South would like me to give a list of the things the Liberal party did while in power I am afraid the minister's estimates would not get through tonight. It would take too long.
Oh, oh.

I was just indicating the supplementary things that still needed to be done notwithstanding what had been done. At Cape Freels North there is a splendid wharf. As a matter of fact, I carved my initials in it on one occasion just so the people would not forget. However, they need a small slipway, it would not cost very much. Here again is a great fishing settlement.
Then at Newtown the minister is doing some dredging this year which is badly needed, for which the people are extremely grateful indeed. At Pound Cove a wharf would be of great help to the settlement. I am afraid there is nothing I can ask the minister to do in Wesleyville that he has not already done. In the main the same thing applies to Valleyfield-Badger's Quay. The minister is building a big shed on the wharf at Valleyfield. That is badly needed. It will be of great assistance and I am very grateful to him for it.
Then we come to Greenspond. As the minister knows, Greenspond is an island. In Greenspond there are people who would like a causeway built to the mainland. I am not going to make any such extravagant request of the minister this evening. However, there are a certain number of rocks in the channel into Greenspond that for some reason or another we cannot seem to get removed. I think there is the best will in the world but somehow or other the rocks keep on being there. If they could be removed this year, it would be deeply appreciated. Then

in addition, the people of Greenspond West feel the need of a wharf in that part of the island. I think that request will be familiar to the minister's engineers as well. Then at Fair Islands last year a splendid wharf was built. A slipway is needed. I would not put this in the deep urgency class but it is something that would be very much desired. A wharf is urgently needed at Silver Fox Island.
Then moving along the coast we come to Hare bay. The minister and I have had a certain amount of correspondence about Hare bay and I have the feeling that he is gradually being softened up about Hare bay. It is a big settlement, an important settlement and a growing settlement. Although it is not generally regarded as a fishing settlement, the decline in the woods operations in the last year or two has made many people anxious to go back fishing if facilities are available. Therefore, on those two counts this would be a good project for the minister to undertake.
Then I come to St. Brendans. St. Brendans again is an island. I regret to say that for some reason or another the people of St. Brendans do not seem able to give me a majority.
Oh, oh.
Notwithstanding that fact, they are very fine people. One recognizes the fact that there have to be some Conservatives in the world.

You don't have to
worry about them.

These people have a wharf that is not adequate to this important settlement. There is one of the other coves in which they would also like a wharf. If the minister could do something to improve the wharf facilities at St. Brendans, that also would be greatly appreciated.
Then we come to Gambo. I might say that Gambo is the birthplace of the premier of Newfoundland. It is celebrated in a good many other ways as well. It is the railhead of the whole of the north side of Bonavista bay. There is tremendous traffic in and out of Gambo. There is a good deal of local feeling that the wharf that is now there is not really adequate.

Why didn't you build it
when you were in power?

Because we were building other wharves that were even more urgently needed, and in very great number.
Then I come to Glovertown. In Glover-town there is a spendid wharf where the Millie Ford is tied up from time to time.
Supply-Public Works Glovertown is a big settlement. It stretches all the way around Alexander bay. It is a large place, larger than most settlements in Newfoundland. The people on the north side of Glovertown also feel the need of a wharf.
Then there is a certain need for repairs to the wharf at Traytown. I do not think that anything is needed at St. Chads. There is a fine new wharf there. But at Burnside they do need a breakwater. This is a relatively small structure and it would also be very helpful to the fishermen in that rather exposed place.
Then, of course, there is Salvage. Salvage is a great historic fishing settlement, one of the most picturesque places in Canada. It is a place which people would travel thousands of miles to see if it were a little better advertised. It is also a splendid fishing centre, but it is also in need of a wharf. I think the minister has some of the particulars. There is one wharf there but, because of the configuration of the place, there is need of another wharf.
Then I understand some repairs are badly needed to the wharf at Sandy Cove. Also a small wharf would be of tremendous help to the fishermen in Upper Happy Adventure. A small slipway would also be of great help in Powell's cove in Happy Adventure. It is all the more important in Happy Adventure because, as the minister well knows, many of the people in Happy Adventure in the past have made their living at working in the national park. Until the park gets thoroughly organized, facilities for the fisheries would be especially helpful.
Then there are two places, one at the edge of the national park and the other across Clode Sound, called Charlottetown and Bunyan's cove. I am going to tell the minister a secret. I got a lift across the sound the other day on one of the minister's boats. I do not know whether the minister knew he had a fleet down there. However, they were kind enough to run me across the sound. I hope he will not discipline them for doing so. I may say it was not done in working hours. I can assure him of that. In both these places it is apparent that they need small wharves. A wharf would be greatly appreciated also at Port Blandford and would be all the more necessary, I should think, on account of the increased traffic that there will be because of the establishment of the national park, I would not pretend that Port Blandford is ever likely to be a fishing centre, but it is a big place and it is going to be a big tourist centre, and I would have thought that this would be a suitable project.

Supply-Public Works
How big?

Well, it is big enough that I would hope the minister, in his spare time, would build a post office there, too. A couple of years ago we built a wharf; I beg the minister's pardon, his department built the wharf at Canning's Cove, and this wharf has been a tremendous boon, not only to the people of Canning's Cove but also to the people of Musgravetown and the people of Bloomfield. Musgravetown and Bloomfield are farm settlements. In fact, they are two of the largest farming settlements in my district which, perhaps, is not the leading agricultural constituency in Canada. These people, however, produce a large quantity of potatoes and other vegetables which they sell all along the northeast coast. At the present time they have to truck these vegetables over some very high hills and steep grades for quite a considerable distance to the wharf at Canning's Cove. In the old days there was a public wharf at Musgravetown. Of course one wharf would serve that place and also Bloomfield; I would not ask the minister for two.
How about a subway?

This wharf would more than justify itself. A small wharf was built on the other side of the bay at Portland last year and it is surprising to note how much use has been made of it. It has stimulated the fisheries in an area which has not been a fishing area. When the minister can get around to it, a wharf would be very helpful at Winterbrook, which is a large centre for the fishing and collection of lobsters. A wharf is very badly needed, indeed, at Southern Bay and also at Charleston. Though these places are fairly close together one wharf would not do for both of them, because there has been a good deal of development in recent years in this whole area with the pothead whale fishery and the squid and herring fisheries. These marine works there would really enormously assist the people to exploit these riches of the sea.
Wharves are needed at Princeton and at Summerville. A wharf was built at Plate Cove West only last year, and there is a wharf at Openhall but the people feel it would be much more useful to them if they could have another block on it. The people of Tickle Cove would like a wharf. I admit that this is a difficult proposition because Tickle Cove presents many problems. It is right on the Atlantic and it will tax the ingenuity of the minister's engineers to produce the kind of structure which will stay there.
I am pleased the minister is undertaking to replace the wharf at Duntara which was

regrettably destroyed by a storm about a year ago, and by so doing he has given heart to the fishermen. I believe Knight's Cove is another place where if a wharf were built there could be considerable development of the fishery, and Upper Amherst Cove is a great fishing settlement. It would be of great assistance to the people there if a wharf could be built to assist in the prosecution of the fishery, making it not only easier but more profitable, and it would, enable them to carry on their activities for a longer period each year. At Newman's Cove I know there are again great engineering difficulties but assistance is also required. In this latter place there is exposure to the Atlantic, but extensions to the present wharf are needed. At the other side of the cove a slipway is badly needed, which I am very hopeful the minister will be able to look after this year. At Birchy cove there is a smaller settlement but everyone who lives there is a fisherman and it would be very helpful if there could be a small slipway and a block built on which to tie the boats.
I am very grateful for what the minister is going to do this year in Bonavista and the people of Bonavista are also very grateful. The completion of the dredging of the pond and the work on the public wharf will be of great help and I hope it can be commenced at an early date. There is, however, one other project at Bonavista which has been under discussion for quite a long time. It is not a big job, but it is something which is clearly a federal responsibility and I hope it might be possible for the minister to consider taking steps in this regard this year, because it certainly is not one of those big works which would have to appear separately in the estimates. I refer to the fixing up of O'Dea's Pond. If my time had not just about expired and if the minister's patience was not wearing a little thin, I could go on to mention a lot of smaller works. I think perhaps I have suggested enough to keep the minister's department busy for the rest of this year and to indicate to him a few of the more important projects which people in Bonavista-Twillingate are very hopeful it will be possible to carry out next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in fairness to the other members of the house, I think I should point out that the practice of my department is to construct projects in inverse ratio to the time taken up by members representing the various constituencies.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on this subject, firstly to thank the Minister of Public Works for what his department has done and is planning to

do in my district. I have in mind particularly the wharves at Tarrington Haven for Happy Valley and Conche.
I would also like to make mention of the high calibre of the officials of his department. I would, in fact, like to pay tribute to all civil service officials in their sincere and patriotic endeavours. The nation, indeed, owes a debt of gratitude to these faithful persons who devote their lives to the public service.
I would now like to mention a number of urgently needed public works for my own riding; firstly, a wharf and shed are needed at Botwood and at Lewisporte. These ports are busy shipping points and such accommodation is vital to their economic health. An extension is also needed to the wharf at Nain, and a fishermen's wharf is required at North West River slipway and a winch at Pinware. Wharves, at Hopedale, Pacquet, Fleur de Lys and Seal Cove need to be lengthened. The canal at Pilley's Island needs to be deepened and consideration should be given to dredging Jim's Cove. At this latter point a wharf is needed or, in the alternative, at Card's Harbour.
Wharves are needed at Embree, Hampden, Baie-Verte, Budden's Tickle in Sop's Arm and extensions are needed at Burlington and Wild Bight. A shed is needed on the wharf at Raleigh. Shove Tickle in Little Bay islands needs dredging and the breakwater should be raised.
In many cases the wharves are more than mere facilities for the handling of freight. They are vital so far as fisheries are concerned and the loss of a landing wharf can mean the ruination of the fisheries for a whole community. Conversely, the provision of such a wharf can mean a real increase in the quantity of fish caught.
Viewed from any angle wharves are of the utmost importance to a riding such as my own, where the sea provides both the means of livelihood and the means of transportation.

Hon. members may not realize it, but in a modest way I am a shipowner, too, although not quite one of the same magnitude as my colleague from Bonavista-Twillingate. Nevertheless I can invite the minister to make a tour of my riding, and I can assure him that the cooking will compare with any he could get on any other ship in Canada, because the cook is my own wife. So I invite the minister to come down and travel with me any time he wishes, and I am sure he will find a lot of appreciative people in my riding of Burin-Burgeo, particularly the fishermen, who will give evidence of their gratitude for the work that has already been done.
Supply-Public Works
There are 260 settlements in my riding. I think the minister has made a sufficiently long tour for one night, so I will not take him over the whole length and breadth of my riding at this time, but I can assure him when I was elected in 1949 and travelled my riding for the first time I compiled a whole shelf full of works to be undertaken, so there is no shortage of requests for public works as far as the minister's department is concerned. In fact I am sure that the district office could provide a whole long list of works which could be put on his shelf, and I think that some have already been on the shelf for a considerable time now.
I wish to make a plea for several settlements in my riding where the people have been obliged to return to the fisheries but cannot carry on the fishery successfully because the harbours have deteriorated to such an extent that they cannot keep their boats in shelter at all. Perhaps hon. members do not realize just how hard a fisherman has to work. In my own birthplace-a little fishing settlement which is typical of others all around the coast-the fishermen get up well before daylight, sometimes around two or three in the morning, get their gear ready and set sail for the fishing grounds. It may take about an hour or two to reach them before daylight. They return at about six o'clock, get a bite to eat, and then have to cut ^ the fish, an operation which takes them until eight o'clock at night. Then, probably, they have to get into their boats and travel ten or 12 miles to get bait for the next day. They return at ten o'clock, or later, and are able to sleep for three hours, or four at the most, before beginning the next day's work. That is one of the reasons why our people grow old before their time and, of course, it is impossible to keep this up indefinitely.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but we are at present discussing the items of the public works estimates. I would ask the hon. member to adhere to the question under debate.

I was only illustrating the need for these minor works which have been referred to by my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate. They may seem trivial to some hon. members, but they are of the utmost importance to fishermen for the reasons I have outlined.
I have in mind, particularly, a place called Seal Cove where there are about 500 people all of whom now are dependent upon the fisheries because those who were formerly engaged in the woods operations can no longer find employment there. This is one place where they cannot do anything this year unless something is done to deepen the water in the harbour.

Supply-Public Works
Around the Lamaline area there are a number of fishing settlements with about 1,000 fishermen. There are scarcely any harbours around that coast and a real need exists for dredging, building breakwaters and erecting other installations to make it possible for these people to carry on the fishery without unnecessary hardship. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the need for sheds at Grand Bank and Fortune. During the election campaign the Minister of Transport announced that these two sheds would be built, but I see that no appropriation has been made for this purpose in this year's estimates. I assure the minister that these sheds are very urgently needed and I hope that the completion of these structures will not be too long delayed.
Before I sit down I should like to say one or two words about St. John's Harbour. I referred to this on the first estimate, but only in a general way. The minister is in possession of a plan which has been prepared by an engineering company and I suppose all plans are based on facts, forecasts and assumptions. The facts would result from surveys which would reveal the actual tonnage of shipping using the harbour, the actual volume of freight handled and the movement of freight between various points; the forecast would be an interpretation of those facts in so far as they might indicate the growth of shipping in the future, increases of freight handled and changes in the movement of traffic; and the assumptions would be with respect to future shipping trends. The assumptions also would relate to what shipping firms would be carrying on business in the harbour and also as to what effect certain harbour installations might have on the ebb and flow of the tide and the undertow in the harbour itself.
In all these factors there is room for a certain margin of error; there is room for error in interpretation of the facts and there is certainly room for a large margin for error in the area of forecasts and assumptions. This was our sad experience at Port aux Basques, though I do not think the Department of Public Works should shoulder all the blame for what happened there. The primary error there was the construction of a ship far too large for the harbour, and the second error was the selection of a site for the terminal which was located in the only place where it should never have been put. If that was done on the advice of engineers, I think we have the right and the duty to question plans that engineers may bring forward because they certainly are not infallible.

The shipping trend in the future must of necessity be in the direction of larger ships because smaller ships cannot operate economically in the light of present day operating costs. As I understand it, the present plan has certain defects in that it provides for the dockage of the larger ships in the narrowest part of the harbour. If the pattern in the future is to get away from small ships and have larger and larger ships in that harbour, then we cannot accommodate all the ships in that place where the one large dock is to be located.
The other defect in the plan is that it reduces the area of the harbour available for anchorage, and this is a serious defect as far as St. John's is concerned, because St. John's is the one harbour where the banking fleet will rush for shelter whenever a hurricane occurs and in the past several years we have had several experiences of that kind when the harbour filled overnight with ships, all sorts of shipping including the banking fleet and coastal ships which had rushed there for shelter. Any plan which would diminish the water surface of the harbour available for that would, in my opinion, be a serious disadvantage.
In addition, the other defect as far as the present plan is concerned is that it reduces considerably the amount of linear footage available for the docking of ships. I do not think that criticism is intended in any way to condemn the present plan, but it indicates that other possibilities should be very carefully looked into before any firm decision is arrived at. The present plan seems to me to have developed either because the company had in mind a fixed expenditure and tried to keep the plan within the limits of that expenditure, or else its survey did not envisage any great future expansion of commerce for the harbour. I do not think any of us can foretell what is going to happen in the next 50 or 100 years, and it would be most unfortunate if we did anything at this time which does not have to be done, and which might turn out in the future not to be for the best.
I do not know what defects the alternate plan has, but I understand it to be much more comprehensive and a much more expensive plan. Furthermore it corrects some of the defects that I have already mentioned. I would certainly urge the minister to give it very careful consideration and if it means expending $20 million or $50 million, not to let the amount of expenditure stand in the way of doing the very best possible job.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the time of the committee for a few minutes to point out to the minister some of the discrepancies in the remarks of my

colleague from Newfoundland, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. He concluded his remarks by saying that the narrow portion of the harbour-I presume he meant the west end of the harbour-would be narrowed down considerably by the construction of a large pier.
Mr. Chairman, I did not say anything of the sort; I am sorry.
Perhaps my hon. friend would clarify it.
I said the present plan makes provision for the docking of ships in the narrowest part of the harbour, in the western part of the harbour.

The point that I would like to clarify for the benefit of the minister and the departmental officials particularly is the fact that deep sea shipping, that is shipping of fairly heavy tonnage, have always in previous years-and there is no reason why they will not do it in future years-used the eastern end of the harbour. I am sure the hon. member will also agree with me when I maintain that there is no reason to believe that, with the construction of this large jetty in the western end of the harbour and the breastwork which will form the basis of the northern side of the harbour of St. John's, there will be anything to stop heavy ships, if any heavy shipping comes to St. John's in the near future, from using the eastern end of the harbour and which now uses the premises of Furness-Withy and Harvey and Company.
By the same token, it has been pointed out by engineers of the Foundation Company of Canada, and various other experts, that the jetty is being built in the western end of the harbour to facilitate the handling of ships up to 10,000 tons. I am sure the hon. member is fully conversant with the facts, and I am sure he is fully aware that since the end of world war II there has been little or no shipping in the harbour of St. John's over 10,000 tons. I am sure the same critics of this plan that the hon. member has quoted and he are aware of the fact the suggestion has been made that this development will make St. John's a sixth rate harbour. I would like to point out that right now we are not even a tenth rate harbour. What I maintain is that when the present plan is implemented it will not be the answer to all of our problems but it will be an improvement and it will, I hope, be the beginning of many more improvements to the harbour of St. John's.
I certainly would like to see this plan started as soon as possible.
Supply-Public Works

Mr. Chairman, what the hon. member for St. John's East has just said I pointed out at the beginning, namely that this survey was based on some facts, forecasts and assumptions. One of the assumptions is that the shipping firms now operating in the eastern part of the harbour will always be operating there. I think that is not a valid assumption. More than that, the very fact which he mentioned, namely in the western end of the harbour there is to be accommodation for 10,000-ton ships, is going to tend to put those shipping firms in the eastern part of the harbour out of business altogether. If it is possible to expand this plan to utilize the eastern part of the harbour, as we are doing now for the western part, then St. John's will not have to be a sixth rate harbour; it will be a first rate harbour.

Mr. Chairman, it would be very unkind of me if I were to say that the people of my riding are not grateful for the work that the Department of Public Works has in hand this year, but I must say that we are not satisfied and we hope that the doors are not closed. We hope that many improvements which could be done at very little cost will be taken in hand. Also, there are many projects which I sincerely hope will receive sympathetic consideration in the not too distant future. At this time I want to publicly thank the Minister of Public Works for the prompt replies that I receive to requests made to him on behalf of the settlements in Trinity-Conception.
In my riding the Department of Public Works proposes to spend $110,000 this year on new construction work in the settlements of Elliston, Little Catalina and Old Shop. But there are many more communities needing facilities to assist fishermen in the carrying on of their work at the fisheries.
I should also like to call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the urgent need of an extension to the wharf at South Dildo, near the premises of the Arctic Fisheries Products Limited, and where the provincial government owns a co-operative plant and O'Brien Fisheries carry on a fisheries business. Here is a very important industry which creates considerable employment for the residents in that area. As a matter of fact, when there is a good fishery there are as many pounds of sea products put through these plants as in many large fishing plants in other parts of the island.
I have presented to the Minister of Public Works several petitions from settlements ir. my riding. However, in addition I have a few more. For instance at Hibbs Cove, Port de Grave, a breakwater is badly needed. The fishermen there have to travel as much as 50 miles per day to get to the fishing grounds

Supply-Public Works Hibbs Cove is one of the biggest fishing settlements in Newfoundland.
There are also many places where wharves should be constructed such as Green's Harbour, Hillview, Lady Cove, Little Heart's Ease, Long Beach, Queen's Cove, Sunnyside, Thornba, Western Bay, Melrose and Trinity East. Trinity East is a growing settlement because many families are moving there from remote areas.
Slipways are required at Blackhead, Lead Cove, Gull Island and Clarenville. Extensions to public wharves are required at Caplin Cove in Trinity bay Cavendish, Chance Cove, Freshwater in Conception bay, Gooseberry Cove, Hant's Harbour, Deer Harbour, Lead Cove, Lower Island Cove, Low Point, Monroe, New Harbour, Old Pelican and Winterton. Dredging is also necessary in many places in my riding, particularly at Cupids where John Guy founded a colony in 1610.
I am sure that the minister of public works will consider these requests. I know that he is unable to fulfil all the requirements of my riding but I feel confident that these requests will receive consideration by his department and what cannot be done this year or next year will probably be done in the near future.

Mr. Chairman, I realize that by this time there is not much room left on the minister's shelf. He said a few moments ago that the amount of work done would be in inverse proportion to the length of the speech and I will take him at his word. I hope when I am finished that the possibility of getting done what we want done will be a probability of at least one project. When the minister is making up his estimates for the coming year I would be very pleased if he would have a look at the need for harbour installations at Port au Port, Ship Cove, Parson's Pond, Corner Brook and St. George's. I have made my remarks short, Mr. Chairman.

348.	New Brunswick, $4,060,500.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take the minister on a tour of all the coves and inlets in Northumberland-Miramichi, but I notice that in the estimates there are only two items, one for $32,000 and the other for $40,000. However, there are a number of places along the coastline of Northumberland-Miramichi which are in need of facilities and in some cases improvements to existing facilities. The fisheries of Northumberland-Miramichi are very diversified, including all the delicacies that come from the sea, and the people of that part of the

riding derive their livelihood from fishing. The minister may not be as familiar as the department is with the requests that have been made in the past for improved facilities and in some cases new facilities where no facilities exist. I urge the minister to take a look at the requests that have been made from time to time in the past. I too would invite the minister to come down to the famous Miramichi river which is often referred to as the Rhine of America. He would probably enjoy his visit very much, much more than he enjoyed the trip he made last March.
I should like to refer to a matter which, while it has nothing to do with any particular item, would, I think, come under rivers and harbours. I would ask the minister to advise me, not necessarily in the house, with regard to the inquiry I made to him concerning the department's policy as to responsibility for the construction of a bridge over the Miramichi river at Chatham. I do not think there is anything more I want to say. I have spoken in general terms. I realize that everything cannot be done in one year but I find that the estimates covering Northumberland-Miramichi are probably less this year than they have been for many years. It may be that will be offset next year by a very good vote and the provision of money for those facilities needed by the fishermen of that area.

Mr. Chairman, I too do not want to take too much time of the committee at this time but I have a few questions which I should like the minister to answer. Instead of making a statement I will simply ask a few questions which I hope the minister will be able to answer. Could the minister advise the committee what the program of the department is in connection with the wharf extension at Maisonnette? I brought this up in my remarks on the first item of these estimates. I mentioned at that time that the minister had a golden opportunity to provide employment in a fishing community. By extension of the wharf at Maisonnette I am sure the fishermen of the area and others would be provided with employment.
I should also like to ask the minister what the present plan is with regard to improvement of Bathurst harbour. I notice an item of $100,000 covering dredging of Bathurst harbour this year but I understand that this item is to cover work done in previous years by departmental dredge No. 4 which I understand has been scrapped by the department this year. Would the minister answer these questions?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
First of all, with regard to Maisonnette; the situation there is that the

department estimates that the cost of providing a 208-foot extension to the existing 290-foot structure, including a small quantity of very costly rock dredging, would be approximately $164,000. Preliminary reports indicate that the commercial activity there would not justify an expenditure of this amount. However, we are having another look at it in order to get a more detailed report.
With regard to Bathurst, the situation there is that shortly after the new government took over we decided that it would be of great advantage to northern New Brunswick if a smelter were to be built at Bathurst. As the hon. member knows there have been very important finds of zinc, I presume in his county or perhaps it is in the adjoining county. However, there was a very promising mine in the province, in a place where it was not expected there would be such large base metal reserves. The mine was in operation, and we decided that we would spend up to $3.5 million for dredging at Bathurst to make it possible to use the wharf to the full extent, providing that the mining company would undertake to erect a smelter, and wharf.
We had very high hopes that they would agree, and I think for some time they were about to commence this project. However, as hon. members know, the price of zinc has fallen a great deal in recent months, and for the time being there is no prospect of the company building a smelter at Bathurst. In fact I think they have closed down their mining operations in recent weeks. This offer by the government still stands. We believe that a base metal smelter at Bathurst would be of immense value to the whole of the maritimes, and would be one of the most important developments that could be undertaken anywhere in Canada. There is power now being produced at Beechwood, and the fact there is cheaper power available is very material in this whole picture.
We have not lost interest in Bathurst harbour. The vote of $100,000 does not replace the other development. As I have already pointed out, we still have in mind going on with the full scale harbour development provided a smelter is erected in Bathurst. I would point out that this $100,000 is to be expended for dredging in Bathurst. There are other expenditures in the hon. member's riding. For example, harbour improvements at Blue Cove will cost $110,000 and breakwater repairs at St. Mary's, $50,000. There may be others, but we are very much interested in Bathurst.

I am pleased to hear the minister say that the offer for improvement 57071-3-92
Supply-Public Works of Bathurst harbour still stands pending action by the mining company. I would hope that in the meantime consideration would be given to the immediate improvement of this harbour, especially wharfage facilities. Bathurst is a shipping port and at the present time there is no public wharf which could be used to advantage by shipping interests.
There are two more questions which I should like the minister to answer. Has any consideration been given to the removal of the old breakwater at the entrance to Tracadie harbour? I mentioned this in my remarks when these estimates were introduced. This old breakwater is definitely blocking the entrance and it is a menace to navigation which could result in the loss of life.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In so far as the possible menace to navigation in Tracadie harbour is concerned, our officials are now estimating the cost of removing the existing north breakwater ruins, and following a review of the report consideration will be given to whatever action is indicated.

Again I wish to thank the minister for this action being taken by his department in relation to Tracadie harbour. My last question is this. On June 13 the minister said that the Chignecto canal was being studied by his department. Is the minister now in a position to report to this committee on what action has been taken by his department in connection with the Chignecto canal?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, the study is still under way.
How far has the study been carried? Have any engineers of the department been instructed to make preliminary plans?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: This study is being carried on within the department, and I am afraid I cannot go any further than that.

Can the minister also
report now as to the progress which has been made in the survey in connection with the New Brunswick-Prince Edward Island causeway?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I would be delighted to talk about that. There is a substantial vote for this item, but I have mislaid my notes. I will be glad to deal with it, when we come to that vote.

349.	Quebec, $4,036,100.

Mr. Chairman, I see that in vote 349, the province of Quebec will receive $4,036,100. The province of Newfoundland

Supply-Public Works will receive $3,640,000; Nova Scotia, $4,057,500; New Brunswick, $4,060,500.1 am certainly glad to see that these provinces are going to get a substantial amount. I see also that Ontario will receive $11,642,900. No doubt the province requires that amount, and I am glad to see they are going to get it. But you will notice that in four provinces you have 74 per cent of a total amount of $31,919,500.
Toronto harbour itself is going to get $4,438,500, which is more than the whole province of Quebec is going to have, namely $4,036,100. I see there is no appropriation for Montreal harbour, for Quebec harbour or for the Three Rivers harbour. As we have a very large number of unemployed at the present time in Montreal, I find it to be rather funny that Montreal and the whole province of Quebec are going to get such a small sum. I was wondering what the minister had to say on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is not possible to allot money on the basis of the proportionate size of the provinces. These problems, of course, are completely different in every province. Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and British Columbia, with their long coast lines, have many maritime harbour problems. Then they may vary from year to year. One year there will be a big project under way in one particular part of the country and smaller ones in another part. It is therefore not fair to review the estimates on the basis of setting out one province against another.
In so far as Montreal is concerned, much to my surprise the hon. member has completely overlooked the fact that Montreal is under the national harbours board and is not under the Department of Public Works at all. The moneys spent on the St. Lawrence river there are spent by the Department of Transport and not by the Department of Public Works at all. If we had all the figures of all the government expenditures on Montreal and Toronto, I think there might be protests coming from Toronto rather than Montreal. However, I do not want to get the members from those two cities fighting it out on the floor of the house. Nevertheless I point out that both Montreal and Quebec are under the national harbours board which does not come under the Department of Public Works at all. This is true also of Three Rivers and Chicoutimi.
Am I to understand from the minister that Toronto harbour comes under the Department of Public Works?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Toronto harbour is under the Toronto harbour commission. It is like quite a few other harbours across Canada. There is a bill coming up at this session to establish a harbour commission at the lakehead which

will cover the harbours of Fort William and Port Arthur. In all fairness to Toronto I must say that although this city has been on fresh water and has been an inland port and will be one, of course, until the seaway is completed, the people there have spent millions and millions of their own dollars to develop the harbour of Toronto. I do not suppose there is another city in Canada which has paid so much good hard cash to build up its own harbour. They do not want to be under the national harbours board. Apparently their wish is to run their own harbour. But the harbour of Montreal, like the harbour in my home'city of Vancouver, has had millions of dollars spent on it by the national harbours board. I do not think that any criticism can be made of Toronto by way of comparison of federal money that has been spent on the Toronto harbour and on other harbours.

The minister says that the port of Toronto comes under the Toronto harbour commission. But if you have $4 million coming from the Department of Public Works there, what would be the equivalent that Montreal would get? If Montreal does not get anything from anybody-and they must, of course-it would be unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: When the hon. member says that Montreal does not get anything from anybody-*
Pardon me, but I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: -may I point out that Montreal is getting millions and millions of dollars. This St. Lawrence seaway development is meaning an expenditure of many millions of dollars in Montreal. As I say, these estimates do not come under the Department of Public Works; they come under the Department of Transport.

That is the point I wanted to make. What would be the equivalent? If you give the port of Toronto $4 million, then Montreal would get the equivalent from the harbour commission. You are not giving Toronto something that you do not give to Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We are not in a position to know that because we have no jurisdiction over the harbour of Montreal.
No comparison can be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

May I first of all tell the minister that I am happy indeed that the government has decided this year to carry out the several projects that were conceived and planned by the previous government. As hon. members know and as does the

minister, my riding lies along the St. Lawrence river, and owing to the heavy navigation a considerable amount of damage has been done to the shore. Over the years a series of retaining walls has been built in order to protect the shore from erosion. I am happy to see that this year the program with respect to retaining walls is being continued. I am particularly happy also to see in the estimates an item for the St. Anne retaining wall. That particular project is an urgent one. It is a residential area of greater Sorel and the shore is quite close to the channel. Over a period of years the lapping of the waves has deteriorated the shore to such an extent that some of the buildings in that particular area have been in danger of being affected by the erosion.
I recall that there were to have been negotiations between the Department of Public Works and the municipality of St. Anne with regard to the reconstruction of that particular wharf. I do not know at what stage the negotiations may be at this date. However, if it were useful for the department, I should be happy to try to arrange for negotiations between the municipality and the department so as to try to get this work done as quickly as possible and certainly , if it were possible, before winter sets in.
There is another item that I should like to mention at this time. It has to do with the improvements of harbours in connection with the St. Lawrence seaway. The seaway, of course, has been expected to bring into Canada an economic potential that we did not have previously. We have a right to expect that the ports all along the seaway will benefit from this great project. Sorel, of course, is one of the ports which does not come under the national harbours board and apparently has not received a great deal of attention in the sphere of harbour improvements. I understand that a secret survey has been made of the different ports that will have to be improved in connection with the seaway. I certainly hope that Sorel is included in that particular survey.
The other day the hon. member for Laurier mentioned the usefulness of having some of the ports increase their grain elevator capacity. I understand, of course, it is not up to the Department of Public Works to increase the capacity of grain elevators already in existence, but in Sorel the North American elevators have plans to double their grain capacity. In order to do so they would have to make some changes on the wharf upon which these elevators are built. As a matter of fact, the North American elevator wharf takes the form of an L, and in order to be
57071-3-92J
Supply-Public Works able to accommodate the larger vessels which we expect will sail on the seaway, one part of that wharf will have to be cut off. This will mean that a new wharf will have to be added in the port of Sorel.
Some years ago preliminary work was done in order to bring about this improvement, and I understand that soundings have been taken in an endeavour to figure out where would be the best location for the new wharf. I would indeed be happy to know what progress has been made with respect to the re-arrangement of the wharf.
I would like to mention very briefly one last point, which subject has been a sore spot for some years. I refer to Ste. Anne's in the St. Lawrence, where there is a series of islands used for a number of generations for the growing of hay. During winter months this ^ hay has always been transported from the islands to the mainland but, as the minister knows, some years ago there was a decision to bring in the icebreaker between the islands to keep the channel open during the winter months. The farmers, therefore, can no longer transport their hay over the ice. This cannot be helped and we would not want to stop progress but it does cause some difficulty because, in order to transport the hay over the water the farmers have to take barges and, owing to the irregular shoreline, it is very difficult for them to put the wagons on scows. I would hope that the minister and his department will seriously consider building some slips at a strategic point so that the farmers can transport their produce in a relatively easy fashion.
This question has been raised previously and has been bounced around between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport. I appeal to the minister to try to find some solution. It is all very well to have these legal conflicts between different departments but it is most unfair for the farmers to be left holding the bag with a very serious resulting loss of crops.
I would conclude by saying that I am very grateful that the department is continuing with the program of public works in this particular area, particularly with respect to the St. Lawrence seaway. If it does what it is expected to do it will bring about a position where navigation will be doubled, as will the erosion along the shore line It would therefore be wise, in my opinion, to do as much of the work on the retaining walls as is possible in the shortest possible time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We will be very glad to look into the projects mentioned by the hon. member. He has mentioned a wharf at Sorel, and

Supply-Public Works on that I would inform him that a few days ago I interviewed a representative of the North American elevator company. This is a very big project and if the dominion government were to do as the hon. member suggests it would cost us from $1.5 million to $2 million to change the wharf. While the wharf does belong to the government it is rented to that company, and is used by that company. Whether we would be justified in spending this amount of money under these conditions I am not yet sure.

Has any economic survey been made before arriving at that particular conclusion? Of course, it is a large amount of money to be spent but, on the other hand, I also feel that one cannot expect to improve harbours without spending money. I had understood that besides the seaway itself, serious consideration was being given to improvement of harbours, and I feel this would certainly be a practical way of improving Sorel harbour, which would bring a good deal of business to that particular area. In this connection I would point out that Sorel is at the junction of the Richelieu and St. Lawrence rivers. There are great possibilities in this area which I hope the minister will seriously consider.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No conclusion has yet been reached, but there is only one company concerned. This is not a question of a general wharf for everybody's use; it is a wharf used by one company. It may be possible to work out some plan under which the company would pay a portion of the cost of any alteration. However, we have the matter under consideration.

Along the same line, the minister has said that his offer of $3.5 million for Bathurst still stands, and I wonder why a similar offer should not be made for the port of Sorel, even if the private company has to pay a share. I do remember the policy of the department has been to ask private concerns to pay at least a share of the cost of a wharf such as this but, surely, if the minister is ready to pay the whole cost of a wharf in Bathurst, New Brunswick, there should be no reason why at least half that offer should not be made to help the port of Sorel.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The work at Bathurst is dredging, and in this case the mining company would be constructing a smelter and would spend something over $20 million.
Could the minister tell the committee whether the preliminary work on the new wharf, such as soundings, etc., is continuing?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Apparently there are many engineering problems in connection with alterations to the pier and the studies have not yet been completed.
But they are continuing?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, that is right.
I have just one more question, and it is about retaining walls. I suppose that regarding this item the same rules apply to the protection works and the retaining walls.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Protection walls as they are ordinarily described come under the vote for remedial works.

If the minister will look in Quebec he will find many retaining walls. I do remember that in the past we had the same kind of item, and I am not questioning it, but I would ask the minister to explain his policy with regard to retaining walls. I know that in the past they were attached to the item of protection works, but there were some big items which were separated.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The larger items are provided by a special vote but the great bulk come under remedial works vote.
My question was, do the same rules for protection work apply for retaining walls built on navigable water. There are many items-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The limitation is described in item 355; to provide for remedial works where damages are caused by, or endanger, navigation or federal government structures. That would apply to the items which are listed under the provincial votes as well as to the items which come under 365.
Do they come under the same rules as protection walls?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
Would the minister explain if the retaining wall in St. Joseph-St. Hyacinthe is built on navigable water?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That work is necessary because of changes brought about by a federal structure which was placed on the opposite side of the river at this point. It comes in the category of federal government structures.

I remember that item very well because I took a personal interest in that case, and it was studied two or three times by engineers and it was found out that it did not come under the jurisdiction of the federal government. We had three reports on that work in previous years. I remember the minister telling me once that we were building some protection works to protect

some Liberal farmers. Now I can tell him he is building one to protect Tory farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the situation is that you were building a protection wall on one side of the river, and we are building a wall on the other. I went into this whole question very carefully; we met a delegation from down there and we looked into the matter very carefully, and what I have said is actually a fact. Because of the work on the other side of the river erosion had been caused on the side where we intended to put a wall, and we decided it was our obligation to do it for that reason.

I want to tell the minister that I am not against it; I am glad this has been given to St. Hyacinthe, but I remember well that two or three studies were made, with the results which I have stated. As an engineer I do not think the technique of engineering has changed in so short a time, and I am quite confident in saying that it has been done this year to protect Tory farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: This is just one more case where we have been improving on the policy of the former government.
Not improving. You have been making accusations about patronage, but here is one example of waste and extravagance.

I should like to submit to the committee that the necessity for this protection wall has been sustained by independent engineers who have stated that the federal structure is responsible for the erosion at St. Joseph.

In reply may I say that the independent engineers are not in charge of the Department of Public Works, and it is not the independent engineers who apply the rules and policy of the department but the chief engineer, the deputy minister and the officials of the department.
And the minister.

Well, Mr. Chairman, the
recommendation of the independent engineer has been accepted by the minister and by the department and it is all to their credit.

One month from today, on July 19, there is a community in my constituency that is going to be having a tremendous influx of people for the very well known lake Superior Rossport fish derby, and every year the remarks are generally the same, that the dock facilities in that particular place are very bad, and inadequate for Rossport even as a fishing village, but in view of the tremendous increase of tourist traffic we have
Supply-Public Works coming in there we are quite dissatisfied. Now I do not think the people of the Port Arthur constituency are wharf lovers, dock lovers or breakwater lovers such as they are in Bonavista-Twillingate, but there are a few improvements which are certainly needed, and if the Minister of Public Works would care to provide them and visit the fish derby at Rossport we could give him the honour of presenting the prizes; he might even win a trip to Jamaica, Hawaii or some other interesting place. This is one item I hope the minister's department will look into-at least repair the dock and, possibly, extend the quay.
Another place in the constituency, outside Port Arthur, where some work needs to be done is the Nipigon river where it flows into the bay. The erosion caused by the tremendous amount of pulp that goes down is presenting a serious problem. Almost every spring the C.P.R. has to post slow orders on its bridge there because of the risk, and I feel, strongly supported by the members of the community of Nipigon, that an investigation should be made at this particular spot to see if some form of retaining wall cannot be put up where the river goes down into the bay. It would have to be a very extensive retaining wall because the river flows very swiftly; the Nipigon river is the largest flowing into lake Superior. This is something that needs to be done because I think eventually it is going to cause a great deal of trouble to the bridges there and of course it increases the silt flowing into Nipigon harbour and increases the dredging problem there.
I wanted earlier in the minister's statement to ask him to give us the distinction between harbour improvements and dredging and I hope he will find time to make it clear, because people at the lakehead cannot quite follow that distinction and it is impossible to follow it from the estimates.
There is one point in connection with dredging that I should like to make. If the minister does come up to the Port Arthur constituency for the fish derby I will try to get him introduced to two gentlemen who claim to be the official representatives of the government in that area. These are the two defeated Conservative candidates. One of those defeated candidates made the announcement before the last election that he had obtained an extension of a dredging contract in the turning basin of the Fort William harbour. I happen to know that the former member-you all remember the Reverend Dan Mclvor-had been very active in pressing for this and I remember that this particular incident got Mr. Mclvor's Irish dander up, and I did not blame him.

Supply-Public Works
Again I would like to return from this specific example to the problem that I presented to the minister before. I know he takes a certain partisan glee in tossing things back and forth, especially to the official opposition. It seems to me there is a definite point of political morality involved in this whole question of announcements of government projects throughout the country. No one could object to the government making an announcement, or to the party which composes the government taking credit for doing things, but when you have defeated candidates posing as the people who actually obtained these things I think you are introducing the whole idea of patronage which the minister is trying to stamp out. I was stunned to read in the paper tonight that the hon. member for Carleton has come out with the statement-and this is on this very point-that he cannot handle all the problems that come to him because the rest of the members in the city of Ottawa are from the Liberal party. Again there is the insinuation that in order to get things done you have to go to a government member; that is the only way you can get something done.
It raises the whole question of patronage, and if the minister is really going to stamp out patronage why can he not stamp out this practice of having defeated candidates make announcements and let us have the announcements made in Ottawa, or made by the divisional engineers in the area, rather than carrying on this old idea? I think in terms of political morality it is necessary that you move that one step farther. After all, it is a very small and pretty cheap advantage.
In connection with harbour improvements at the lakehead, I have already made representations to the department that certain kinds of rock work will have to be done within the next two years in the lakehead harbour. I know that that will by and large be a problem of the lakehead harbour commission that is to be set up. I hope you are not chatting about political morality with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He set us back a decade in some ways by that long oration of his tonight.
The rock work that will have to be done in the lakehead harbour is such that it has been proved feasible in the past to do it in the winter time. As hon. members know, we have an unemployment problem every winter in Port Arthur and Fort William and the truck work and the rock-breaking work and the placing of the rocks could be done quite adequately in the winter. I would like to remind the minister that this is something I hope he is planning for right now in so far as next winter is concerned because the

work will have to be done sooner or later and we are going to have an unemployment problem.
There is one point on the lakehead terminals which I would like the minister to clear up and it is in a sense a harbour improvement. Why is there nothing in the estimates for that project? When the minister made his opening remarks on his estimates he made the announcement that Port Arthur and Fort William were going to get $3 million or $4 million spent on them, and also that there was going to be a group of engineers working on the project? Where is the money for those engineers and for that engineering study? It is not that I am distrustful of the minister, but I would like to know where the money is coming from for the initial work on this project? It is very important.
I should like to touch on another point which I brought up earlier and on which I was unable to get an answer from the minister. I can speak on it in connection with this wharf or dock at Kenora. It has to do with the question of the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act and prevailing rates on public works projects and the liaison between the Department of Labour and the Department of Public Works. When a contractor puts in a tender is it perfectly clear in his mind that if he does not pay the prevailing rate he can be forced into it by the government, and that cost will be added to the contract, or will it be added to the contract and be recoverable, or is it a loss that he will have to absorb himself? These are the general questions I wanted to put to the minister. I would like to ask him some further questions. I see the hon. member for Fort William is in his seat; he can ask his own questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Department of Labour polices those contracts. In so far as the questions of losses that the hon. member has mentioned are concerned, if it is necessary for the contractor to pay a higher rate, then that is his loss; the Department of Public Works does not have to make up the difference.
With regard to the harbour developments at the lakehead, we have already engaged an engineering firm to draw up plans and the reason there is no vote is that the expense of the engineers is covered in one of the other votes. There is no vote for the actual construction yet because the plans have not been completed. The hon. member need have no fear, we are going ahead with the development at the lakehead and a very large and important development it will be.

In regard to defeated candidates making announcements, here I think the hon. member is being a little hypersensitive. Nobody knows anything about those jobs until the tenders are called and then they are common knowledge, printed and published in the papers. The tender call is published and some people are active and interested in the work of parliament, interested in getting themselves elected, and they naturally try to follow these things very closely.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps if the hon. member had kept closer to the proceedings he would have got the information himself. Certainly there is nothing secret about it. The work of the department is an open book. The hon. member obviously was not hurt very much by anything that the defeated candidate did to him in Port Arthur.
I think the minister is shying away from what I still think is a point of political morality.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
We do not make a practice of notifying defeated candidates, but if anybody wants to write in and make inquiries we do our best to advise them of what is going on.
The hon. member for Levis asked me for the number of additions to the staff of architects and engineers since July 1 of last year. There are 36 more engineers, 11 of them being in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. There is an increase of seven in Banff-Edmonton and 10 in Ottawa. Then there are other minor changes.
Are they full-time engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Most of these were three to five years. As to the architects, there is only one more now than there was on July 1 of 1957.
I misinformed the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo about what would happen where tenders were called for furniture in a government building in St. John's, Newfoundland. I said that the tender call would go out from Montreal but it goes out from Ottawa.

speechtext: I wonder whether the leader could tell us what is proposed, not merely for tomorrow, because I think that is common knowledge, but for the beginning of the week.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, an arrangement has been reached among the three parties that the private members' day set for next Monday will be postponed. That will make it possible for us to take the budget debate all next week. I am hopeful that we can get agreement to a one day supply motion on the following Monday. Then we would go on and finish the budget debate a week from next Wednesday. July 1 comes on Tuesday and while it is the intention to sit on that day there may be an adjournment for a period of time. I believe a ceremony is taking place on the grounds and we do not want to have the final vote on July 1. That is just tentative. It may be that we will not be able to reach agreement with the parties concerning a week from Monday, but all next week is to be the budget debate. As the first business tomorrow we would like to get third reading of the bill to amend the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act.
